title: Om namah shivaya
hook: the five syllables; what they point at

segments.voice: Yesterday, ishta: the chosen one, and the mantra that comes with it. Your line was one that fits. Did the one you picked come back on its own? Today, the first of four mantras: Shiva's. Day one hundred five.

You heard it on Shivaratri, the great night: temples full until dawn, and one sound rolling through them, over and over. Om Namah Shivaya. It's probably the most widely chanted mantra in the world of Shiva. It's painted on trucks in India, carved over temple doors, whispered by people who've said it a million times, and sung by people who just learned it. It's short. It's easy to say. And it has a hidden count inside it. Five syllables, and each one, people say, is doing something.
screen: `THE SOUND OF SHIVARATRI.` → `ON TRUCKS, ON TEMPLE DOORS.` → `FIVE SYLLABLES INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Take off the Om at the front, and count what's left. Na. Mah. Shi. Vaa. Ya. Five syllables. That's why it's called the panchakshara, the five-syllable mantra. Om is the sound we met on the very first days, the whole of reality in one breath. Namah means I bow. Shivaya means to Shiva. So: Om, I bow to Shiva. It's very old. In the Yajur Veda, in a long hymn called the Shri Rudram, you'll find the words namah shivaya cha shivataraya cha: bow to the auspicious one, and to the more auspicious. That's the root of it. And the name Shiva itself means kind, auspicious, the one who brings good. Now, what does it point at? Here's where teachers have gone deep. In the Shaiva tradition of the south, the five syllables are often matched to the five elements: earth, water, fire, air and space. So saying it is like naming the whole world and bowing to what's in all of it. Others hear the five as five things Shiva does: creating, sustaining, dissolving, hiding and revealing. And there's an old wordplay people love: namah heard as na mama, not mine. Bowing means: this isn't about me. Different teachers hold different meanings, and nobody has to pick one. What most would agree on is where it leads: Shiva as the great yogi, sitting utterly still on the mountain. Saying his name is bowing to that stillness. Your line puts it simply. I bow to the stillness.
screen: `NA, MAH, SHI, VAA, YA.` · `OM, I BOW TO SHIVA.` · `FIVE ELEMENTS, FIVE ACTS.` · `NA MAMA — NOT MINE.` · then, large: `I BOW TO THE STILLNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: japa, twenty-seven times. Japa means repeating a mantra, counting as you go. Twenty-seven is a quarter of a full mala, a string of prayer beads. If you have beads, use them. If not, use your fingers: touch each finger joint with your thumb as you go. Sit, breathe once or twice from your routine. Then, softly, on the out-breath: Om Namah Shivaya. One. Again: two. Let it be slow. If you don't pray, just let it be sound, and count. When you reach twenty-seven, stop, and sit in what's left. The bell holds the time.
Om namah shivaya. Om, I bow to Shiva. Five syllables, na mah shi vaa ya, bowing to the stillness.
Your line: I bow to the stillness. Today, when you catch a still moment, the kettle before it boils, the car before you get out, bow to it, just inside. Day one hundred five.

howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva chant Om Namah Shivaya daily, often 108 times on a mala of rudraksha beads, and sing it through the night on Maha Shivaratri; it is widely chanted openly, though some lineages also give it formally at initiation.

original.note: Sanskrit: Om, I bow to Shiva. The panchakshara, five syllables after the Om.

trapdoor: what you thought: a chant from yoga class.
what it means: Om, I bow to Shiva: five syllables, bowing to the stillness at the center of things.
what a scholar hears: the panchakshara, rooted in the Shri Rudram of the Krishna Yajur Veda; in Shaiva Siddhanta its syllables are mapped to the elements and to Shiva's five acts.
